name: The Critic — Content Rubric (starter)
what_this_is: This is the CONTENT RUBRIC. It grades a piece of CONTENT. It is the material participants extend and build their reviewer around — it is not the rubric used to grade the teams. That is the separate Judging Rubric.
note_to_participants: This rubric is deliberately incomplete. It checks whether content is competent. It does NOT check whether content is right for a specific audience — which is the hard part. Add at least two criteria of your own in 'participant_criteria' below.

values.label: Fail
values.meaning: Actively wrong or harmful to the reader.

values.label: Weak
values.meaning: Present but unreliable. A reviewer would send it back.

values.label: Adequate
values.meaning: Acceptable. Not memorable, not a problem.

values.label: Strong
values.meaning: Does the job well enough to publish as-is.

scale.why: A 1-10 scale makes an AI reviewer cluster everything at 7-8. Four choices with written anchors forces a real decision.

evidence_required.rule: Every score MUST quote the specific text that justifies it. No quote, no score.
evidence_required.why: This is the single strongest defense against a reviewer that praises content it did not actually read.

fatal_criteria.rule: If any criterion marked 'fatal' scores 0, the verdict is REJECT — no matter how high the total.
fatal_criteria.why: Stops '3 + 3 + 3 + 0 = pretty good.' One hallucinated fact is not offset by nice formatting.

the_plus.rule: Any criterion scoring 0 or 1 MUST come with a specific, actionable fix. Not 'improve clarity' — what to change, where.
the_plus.why: Walt's rule: the note has to make the work better, not just say it's bad. A score with no fix is not a review.

abstain_allowed.rule: A reviewer may return 'INSUFFICIENT CONTEXT' for a criterion instead of guessing.
abstain_allowed.when_to_use: Use it when a claim cannot be checked from anything you were given. An unverifiable capability, an uncited figure, or a named system that appears nowhere else are all abstention cases, not average scores.
abstain_allowed.why: Slide 9 block 7: bad evals are worse than none. Guessing is how false greens happen.

starter_criteria.name: Accurate
starter_criteria.question: Is every factual claim true, current, and verifiable?

anchors.0: Contains a claim that is false, or a product/feature/capability that does not exist.
anchors.1: Claims are probably true but stated with more confidence than the source supports — including any capability presented as existing that you cannot verify from the content, the style guide, or the audience card.
anchors.2: Claims are accurate and verifiable; a few could use a citation.
anchors.3: Every claim is accurate and traceable to something real.

starter_criteria.watch_for: Confident tone is not evidence. Check the claim, not the delivery. A capability you cannot verify is NOT a 2 — score it 1, or return INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT. Scoring an unverifiable capability as 'adequate' is the single most common route to a false green.

starter_criteria.name: Clear
starter_criteria.question: Can the reader follow it on one pass, without re-reading?

anchors.0: Incoherent, or steps are in an order that cannot be followed.
anchors.1: Requires re-reading. Jargon appears before it is defined.
anchors.3: Genuinely easy to follow; complexity is sequenced well.

starter_criteria.watch_for: Fluent writing that says nothing still fails this.

starter_criteria.name: Right level
starter_criteria.question: Does it assume the knowledge this audience actually has — no more, no less?

anchors.0: Unusable for this audience — far too advanced or far too basic.
anchors.1: Noticeably mispitched; the reader will be lost or bored in places.
anchors.3: Precisely pitched to the audience card.

starter_criteria.watch_for: Read the audience card before scoring this. It is the most-skipped step in the whole exercise.

participant_criteria.instructions: Add criteria that get at what the starter content rubric cannot see. The starter checks whether content is COMPETENT. Yours should check whether it is RIGHT — for this audience, this intent, this brand.
must_include: a 'question' a human could answer without your content rubric
prompts_if_stuck: Would the intended reader actually be able to DO something after reading this?
Does it sound like us, or like a generic AI assistant?
Is anything important missing that this audience would expect to find?
Does it earn trust — are strong claims supported?
Would this reader feel talked down to, or shut out?
bad_examples: 'Grammar' — the starter already covers competence, and it will not catch plausible-but-off.

verdict.method: Weighted average of all criteria, then apply gates.
gates: Two or more criteria at 1 or below -> REVISE (minimum).
Any criterion returned as INSUFFICIENT CONTEXT -> cannot be SHIP; escalate to human.

thresholds.SHIP: Weighted average >= 2.5 and no gate triggered.
thresholds.REVISE: Weighted average >= 1.5, or any gate short of reject.
thresholds.REJECT: Weighted average < 1.5, or a fatal gate triggered.

output_contract.why: All three build levels must emit this same shape. That is what makes one Judging Rubric work across every submission, whether it was built in Cowork or VS Code.

criteria.fix: required when score <= 1; specific and actionable

self_check.why: Ask your reviewer these before you submit. Slide 9 block 7: a bad eval is worse than none.
questions: Run the same piece twice. Do you get the same verdict? If not, your criteria are too vague.
Did it SHIP anything that a careful human would send back? That is a false green — the worst failure mode.
Did it REJECT anything genuinely good? That is a false red — it creates rework and people stop trusting it.
Does every score quote real text from the content?
Could a person who is not a content expert read your output and act on it? (Slide 9, block 4 — this is the actual bar.)
